en: Om, salutations to Śrī Sundaragaṇapati. [The section on] the beating of the drum and so forth, verse 32397.
(First Page) (First Part) May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to Vikaṭacakravināyaka.
[Salutations] to him who bestows the desired fruit upon even the undisciplined, and who is consecrated as the cutter away of all kinds of obstacles. (Second Part)
I take refuge in him who eclipses the sun with his golden earrings and who possesses a formidable discus and the elephant-headed Vināyaka.
(Third Part) The invocation of the deities, accompanied by the goddess Kāmākṣī;
may there be auspiciousness.
(f1.a, first line)

May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds; may the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of others. May the gods attain peace, and may the entire world be happy everywhere. May the rain-cloud pour forth in due season, and may the earth abound with crops.
May this land be free from agitation.
May the Brahmins be fearless; may the king be devoted to righteousness; may the subjects be of virtuous conduct; may the wealthy honor the good;
and may the twice-born, preeminent in the six duties, daily [cultivate] knowledge and wisdom.
May all be free from agitation and full of bliss, with speech ever-present and the senses turned away from vice;
may they be devoted to the worship of Śiva, delighted by goodness and contentment; and may they honor the teacher who initiates them into learning as if he were Lord Viṣṇu himself.

I bow to the son of the Moon, who is cherished by the wise, whose hearing extends far, whose eyes are wide, who removes the obstacles of the universe, who possesses supreme knowledge, who is the leader, who has the face of an elephant, and who delights in the lute and other musical instruments.
He who is devoted to the rites of dance and song,
who is consecrated in the glorious festival of Yati for the purpose of protecting the three worlds, and who, for that very purpose,
[performs] the life-story of Maheśa at the summoning of all the immortals.

...we celebrate with great joy the sounds of *līlīmarda*, *latā*, *kāhala*, *rīḍakkā*, and other instruments made of bell-metal (*kāṃsyādi*), along with lutes (*vīṇā*), flutes (*veṇu*), clay drums (*mṛdaṅga*), conchs (*śaṅkha*), and kettledrums (*paṭaha*). In the center of the *bherī* drum, on the right and left sides of Śambhu, is Viṣṇu.
May Brahmā, the Prajāpatis, the gods, the Kīlas, all the Mothers,
the great Nāgas, the two worlds, and the two deities Moon and Sun—
for the welfare of those dwelling in the sky, on earth, and in heaven, and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods residing in the netherworld— [protect us].
I now beat the great drum for the satisfaction of the eighteen Gaṇa-deities and the hosts of beings, both moving and unmoving; come, O Śiva-yāga-tīrtha, worthy of being served!

I strike the drum that is a limb of the procession, which has been sounded according to the prescribed rite during an auspicious time— first striking it in sequence with the *Brahmajajñāna* mantra— at the end of the sixth day and at the hour of the night when the fatigue of the journey has subsided.

This is for the purpose of the festival of the drum at the departure for the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), while the hosts of sages, the *Pauṣāca* spirits, and the *Apsarases* follow upon their path, O Murāri.
One should strike the second opening of the drum with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" in due order; proclaiming the glory of all the gods before [the assembly], [he should strike] the entire world...
I strike this drum, which heralds the swift commencement of Śambhu’s festival and establishes the playground of Lakṣmī, by the command of the daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
One should strike it three times in succession with the *triyambaka* mantra. Śrīkaṇṭha has subdued his enemies.
May the cows, the source of prosperity, be content for a long time and capable of providing milk;

may the castes, endowed with various riches, wander about fully satisfied; may there be desirable rain from the heavens; and may the earth, the mother of all crops, be free from drought, while the people remain ignorant of sorrow.
The hosts of gods on earth,
experts in the Śaiva scriptures,
[composed] commentaries with concise summaries.
The auspicious rite of Maṅgalaka was performed, accompanied by the resonant sounds of various conchs and many drums;
it was marked by the fatigue of women hurrying with haste as their servants, overcome with joy, offered prostrations and measured breath-control (prāṇāyāma).

It was adorned with various silken cloths, soft and delicate, and graced by a magnificent, lofty royal banner; it was as majestic as a principal mountain range, enchanting with rows of palaces of equal height, and possessed vast halls and courtyards filled with *vīdhī*, *kāyūdhikā*, *mallikā*, *mālatī*, and other such flowers.
[He who is] intent on embracing and obstructing the *lalita* creeper, [and who is] mounted upon another, amidst a multitude of blossoming flowers from various other trees, both mature and otherwise.

In that city of Maṅgalāvatī, which was free from obstacles and whose outskirts were fragrant with the multitude of mountain peaks stirred by the wind carrying the scent of scattered *paramandāra* flowers,
there was a display of architectural artistry consisting of various pavilions, gate-towers, walls, and other structures arranged without interval within its interior.

In that place where the sweet, low-voiced warbling of flocks of birds was released from their wings— wings that were lovely and bowed down by the weight of a multitude of words of wonder and amazement—
and which was adorned with ten thousand controlled archways;

In that place, where the rows of celestial courtesans belonging to Rudra were engaged in singing and dancing; which was adorned by the mass of rays from the jewels of their ornaments, appearing like a double morning sunlight;
and which was embellished by the clusters of rubies set upon the surfaces of the jeweled crowns of the hosts of gods as they moved about.
In that [city] densely packed with various ornaments,
where a great multitude of people was gathered by a host of young Brahmins who were masters of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas,
he observed the public displays of pleasure and sport manifested on the ramparts.

His curiosity aroused, he played with young men of his own age in the water, delighting in the preparation of fragrant unguents, while engaging in various sports with dolls fashioned from clay upon a stage prepared by the women.

In that city, the circle of the sky was darkened by the mass of various thick clouds of smoke from the sacrificial fires offered by hosts of eminent twice-born men— initiated into the manifold rites of the Aṣṭamī, Atirātra, Aptoryāma, Vājapeya, Pauṇḍarīka, and other great sacrifices— who were presided over by the most excellent Adhvaryu priests.

In that supreme realm where living beings are never oppressed, there dwells a multitude of birds— crows, ruddy geese, ducks, cranes, and swans— with their wings outspread, moving about at will amidst a collection of pure lotuses.

In this city of Śrī-Kāñcī, which is like a lotus pond where the fragrance is intensified by the gentle breeze carrying droplets from the clusters of nectar flowing from the filaments of the pollen of the gods, and which is adorned with the splendor of the illustrious royal realm characterized by manifold forms of prosperity; [The rest of the text follows: ...in this [city], the illustrious Rājarāṣṭra... [etc.]

The sounding of the auspicious drum for the great festival of the increase of longevity, health, all sovereignty, and good fortune; the activity [of the king] who is skilled in the protection of the entire vast world, and who is graced by the lovely sprout-like hand of the daughter of Dakṣa (Dākṣāyaṇī). O Gīrvāṇa! (f5.a, 1st line)
Of the illustrious Ekāmranātha, together with Śrī Kāmākṣyambā— whose body is made beautiful by the spreading mass of luster from bracelets set with clusters of royal gems—
the auspicious commencement, beginning with the striking of the drum and the hoisting of the banner, was performed on the thirteenth lunar day of the month of Dvitīrthā.

During the procession of the vehicle of the Gaṇas, who are expert in providing protection through service to the feet of Śiva— the cause for warding off obstacles to the great festival— which purifies the world: then,
Rudra is on the middle petal of the Śivāstra, Brahmā on the right petal, and [Viṣṇu] on the left petal.
O Pārvatī, Viṣṇu is in the *pālikā* vessel; Sarasvatī is on the southern petal, Lakṣmī on the northern petal, and the Mothers on the eastern petal.
Jyeṣṭhā is on the western petal, Durgā on the northern petal, and Gajānana (the elephant-faced one) is at the mouth of the *kambha*.
Skanda is at the region of the pot; Daṇḍaśāstṛ at the tip of the staff; Caṇḍabhānu in the middle of the staff; and Caṇḍeśvara at the base of the staff.
At the base of the trident are the eleven Rudras, and surrounding that are the twelve [Ādityas].

May the eight Vasus in the eight directions, the deities of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī surrounding them, and the eighteen Gaṇa-deities together with the Kṣetrapālas— each joined by their respective vehicles, weapons, and retinues— grant their grace.
[This is] the pedestal for the construction of a temple, including the invocation of the deities of well-being,
the installation of pigeons’ feet, the erection of a caitya, and the primary moonstone pillar.
The Prayadarśana [temple] has a square base, an octagonal middle section, and sixteen-sided upper portions; it is adorned with a *kumbha*, *kalaśa*, *vīraka*, *kaṇṭha*, and *kapotaka*;

it possesses variegated leaf-patterns, waves, *antaravājī* [arches], scales, paths, and victory-ornaments; and its pinnacle consists of a *tīkā*, *enukāyataka*, *pāta*, and a series of *prastara* cornices.

Śālakarṇa, Kūṭapañcanāsikā, Mahānāsikā, Śravakulabhūṣaṇa, Grīvāśikhara, Sthūpivarga, Drāviḍa, Vesara, Nāda, Rādiveja, Śrīpīṭhaka, Svastikarṇa, Śrīkailāsa, Meru, Mandara, Nalina, Kapralina, Gajasiṃha, Nandyāvarta, Nāmagaṇḍimālālaṅkāra, Jagatī, Candrakalpavṛkṣastha, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Narasiṃha, Brahmavṛṣasthalamaka.
The gateway arches,
the lotus stalks of the railings, the intermediate space, the celestial realms, the forms of liberation, the ninety-six types of divine palaces, and the assembly halls of the retinue.

[It was] guarded by door-keepers residing facing the gate-towers and palaces at the edge of the sacred seats (pīṭha), [and frequented by] the gods headed by Indra, the sages with faces turned upward, Garuḍa, Gandharvas, Kinnaras,
Kiṃpuruṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Haṃsas.

May the presiding deities, together with their abodes consisting of five divine walls adorned with garlands and gate-towers, become present here. (Line 2) May he who stands facing Śiva, fortunate by virtue of his swift strides upon the excellent peaks that are characterized, sharp, and exceedingly lofty, [be present].
The preeminent among draft animals,
his neck-ornament bells jingling with a *ghaṇaghaṇa* sound, [the air] was made resonant by the tinkling of small bells (*kiṅkaṇī*) inlaid with clusters of lovely gold and jewels.

Adorned with many kinds of ornaments, possessing beautiful caves and gentle slopes, he is born from a portion of the divine Śrī Viṣṇu; his face is exceedingly serene even when eating various grains such as mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas, and he is born from the thirty-three crores of deities who were struck with awe by his long, dark form. May the presence of the deity Śrī Vṛṣabha... be [established].

May He perform [this rite]—He whose independent mental resolve is constrained by the machinery of creation, maintenance, and destruction, which brings about the power and status of all the foremost gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra; who consists of the eternal and pure knowledge whose objects are the reality of all things in the three times of past, future, and present; whose form is the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) consisting of phonemes, words, mantras, worlds, principles, and kalās; and who dwells within the interior of Mount Mandara, amidst the circle of the moon and the sun that are being beheld... [End of fragment]

The one who has cast out the lamp [of ignorance]; who delights in the sport of bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation upon his devotees; who resembles a rain-cloud filled with water by means of the multitude of rays flickering from the poison in his throat.

Possessing a luster that has eclipsed the blackness [of the Kali age], his pair of lotus feet are within the range of vision of the navel and eyes of the Boar-incarnation, whose face is made terrifying by tusks as white as autumnal clouds;
they are rendered most brilliant by the white ash, pure as a shower of nectar from the whitest crystal.
His body is radiant, his manifold manifestations are perfected by five faces, ten arms, and fifteen eyes;
in his right hands he holds a tomara-weapon, a spear, a trident, a sword, a mace, and a serpent; in his left hands he carries a *pināka* bow, a skull-topped staff, a shield, a skull-cup, and a noose.

The multitude of elephants, deafening the quarters with the deep resonance arising from the continuous hollows of their temples, delighted the assembly of gods headed by Indra with their skillful inquiries regarding the welfare of the mountain.
Mounted upon a great bull and other forms praised by the host of Rākṣasas, with the rays of the crescent moon resting upon the peak of his matted-lock crown,
he is the one who uproots the darkness and extinguishes the world’s heat of sorrow; adorned with earrings that shimmer like jewels, his forehead is graced by the brilliance of precious gems.
With his pair of ears turned crimson, with the radiance of his forehead-eye blazing forth, with a garland of skulls draped across his chest,
and with a body that has conquered the five-arrowed god of love— he is Śaṅkara, the bestower of fearlessness upon the world.
May the presence of Śrī Rudramūrti Śivāstra reside within the middle petal of the trident. 4.

...resplendent with a sacred thread (*upavīta*) resembling a continuous string of lotus fibers produced by the current of the river of blood falling upon the multitude of peaks of the Golden Mountain (*Kanakaśikharin*), ...whose chest was adorned with a garland of *kalavegu* flowers. (Fragmentary) ...the Lord of Ascetics (*bhūtapati*).

He whose four lotus-like hands held a book, a rosary, a water-pot, and bark garments— hands praised by all the gods, including the preeminent bird-vehicle [Garuḍa], for his skill in protecting the entire realm of moving and unmoving beings; he who was adorned with his own eight very clear eyes like white lotuses.
And furthermore,
he is the progenitor of Sarasvatī, whose body is as beautiful as a collection of delicate loveliness white as the jasmine flower and the crescent moon, and who possesses a mandala of four faces.

May he, who is intent upon the breaking of the fast by tasting the nectar-like essence of the yoga of meditation on Śiva according to his own will; who is present upon the southern petal of the divine trident of Lord Śiva, the deity of Brahman; who is skilled in protecting all beings through the grace of the Great Lord—whose nature consists of manifold manifestations such as earth, water, fire, air, ether, smell, taste, form, sound, and touch, which are yet non-different from the auspicious Bhava; and who holds the conch, discus, mace, sword, and other [weapons]—[may he grant protection]. 5. May he, who is expert in the preservation of all the world through the compassion of Maheśa, whose self is the manifold play of existence divided into the distinctions of earth, water, fire, wind, space, smell, taste, form, sound, and touch; and who bears the conch, discus, mace, sword, and so forth...

He whose lotus-like hands shine, adorned with various divine weapons; who, with his three strides, traversed the entire surface of the earth; who bore the burden of the multitude of all cosmic eggs held within his own belly; whose prowess crushed the pride of the serpent-king who had assumed the form of a mountain; whose vehicle is Garuḍa; from whose beautiful navel-palace, as lovely as a captivating lotus, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was born; and who submerged the son of Kaśyapa (the serpent Śeṣa) in the midst of all the oceans.

He who assumed the form of a boar for the sake of upholding and protecting [the earth]; he who took the form of a formidable tortoise, becoming the support for the entire world; he who performed the sport of the Fish Incarnation, rendered multicolored by the mass of various waves tossing upon the vast great ocean; he whose sharp tips of claws were expanded by the unbearable prowess of Śarabha and Siṃha, and who shattered the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu, from which flowed a stream of blood that nourished the emerald mountain (Giriśaila); he who is the kinsman of the mountain.
His neck and shoulders are enchanting;
his chest is smeared with sandalwood paste from the slopes of the breasts of the Goddess of Fortune who dwells in the lotus-palace;
he is the most fierce and powerful pillar supporting the entire universe.
With four arms and staff-like limbs, his entire world protected by the command of the Supreme Lord,
he is the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa, devoted to partaking in the nectar of the yoga of meditation upon Śiva, holding the divine trident— the weapon of Śiva— in his left hand.
May he grant his presence. 6.
She who holds in her lotus-like hand a jewel that has doubled its crimson luster by the rays of the rubies in the mass of claws curved like a parrot’s beak;
she who grants fearlessness to the world through the chatter of the parrot held there; and she who is a royal swan in the lotus-pond of the hearts of the sages.
Bearing the weight of the jar-like breasts filled with the nectar of breast-milk, which overflowed with supreme bliss ignited by the tasting of the lotuses of his wife’s face,
he was adorned with a blue lotus fastened to the region of his waist for the sake of his wife.

The sun of the radiance of her sidelong glances, which are beautiful due to the loveliness of every part and filled with compassion; the moon whose orb is eclipsed by the splendor of the luster of her face; the burner of the sins arising from worldly existence.

The mass of her lovely, curly locks— rendered beautiful by the cooling of the continuous heat that torments all the people of the world with its garland of flames— dispels swarms of bees; while the clusters of blossoms, made golden by the humming of bees hovering over them, cause the expansion of the wandering bees to turn tawny.

(First line) With the pair of his lotus-feet made resonant by the accumulation of wandering [bards], he causes the multitude of his slender limbs to be revealed within the space of his body; (Second line) he bestows the power of sovereignty upon others who are subject to his will.

May the presence of the venerable Parameśvarī Śivā—whose mass of fourteen worlds is beautified by the splendor of her own form as she contracts it, and who shines with the majestic power of the lion-vehicle that is capable of bearing the circle of the universe within the quarters of space shaken by the roar of her voice; and whose body is the edge of the divine trident, the weapon of Śiva—grant us her proximity. 7.
The autumn moon, with its splendor rivaling the beauty of moonlight, resembles a mass of conchs from the ocean of nectar;
it reveals her own girdle of jewels and the supreme luster of her gems, manifesting her vow of celibacy through the fresh lotus stalks.

Her body was draped with a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) consisting of a string of beads; she possessed four full arms holding a rosary (*akṣamālā*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a book of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), and a manuscript;
her broad forehead was adorned with a multitude of various beautiful jewels, from which issued a mass of fragrant perfumes wafting forth in dense streams.
May she who possesses the splendor of the sun at dawn,
who is expert in all the Vedas, Śāstras, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and the sixty-four auspicious arts for the protection of the entire world, protect us for a long time.
May the goddess Śrīsarasvatī, who holds a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a divine trident, grant her presence at the base of the right petal of the heart-lotus. 8.

(4th line) A mass of sweet, overflowing nectar, exceedingly heavy with the dripping honey from the thick, matted locks formed by the clusters of celestial tree branches fixed upon the surface of his crown inlaid with fresh jewels;
(5th line)

Her speech is skilled in bestowing upon the world the power of all-encompassing welfare through sounds produced by swarms of bees hovering nearby; she wears armlets, earrings, crest-jewels, pendants, and jasmine garlands that are incomparable and perfectly symmetrical; and she is adorned with necklaces, neck-chains, and golden girdles.
Adorned with various ornaments such as beautiful bracelets, armlets, and anklets, she performs diverse amorous sports upon the pleasure-pavilion of the chest of the Slayer of Madhu.

Those whose own minds are not subject to the influence of others, whose feet possess the beauty that bestows the transformations of the lotus-eyed Lord, who have dispelled the manifold world-illusion,

who have shattered the flashes of lightning-like pride through the manifestation of their own fortune by the multitude of merits earned through their deeds, and who are mines of the light of the Goddess of Eloquence— [to them I bow].
May she who dwells in the lotus, whose pair of lotuses are radiant, who holds a water-pot and a divine trident, grant her presence at the base of the leaf on the left side of Śiva. 9 (5th line)

He is praised by hosts of sages, including all the Siddhas and Sādhyas, who have gathered at the time of sporting within the intervals between the slopes of the Meru, Mandara, Niṣadha, Nīla, and other principal mountain ranges;
he has manifested the faces of the quarters through the overwhelming splendor of his own majesty and power, and he is most intent on destroying all the misfortunes and calamities of the entire world.
The sun that dispels the dense darkness of the multitude of formidable obstacles; the trunk of his trunk extended in play by his own intense and untrammeled bliss.

He who is delighted by the continuous streams of praise proclaimed by the multitude of outward-turned gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, who were seized with terror at the sight of the entire flood of the ocean surrounded by lotuses; he whose universal sovereignty is borne by a steed as white as gold refined by the moon— the treasury of nectar— expert in the consolidation of the entire cosmic egg.

May Vighneśvara— the lord of obstacles, whose two flanks are graced by the service of the entire host of Gaṇas, who shines with splendor, and who is accompanied by Śivā, the trident, the divine water-pot, and other [emblems]— be present here! May he, whose own body possesses a beauty of color like that of a blooming kusumbha flower, who is resplendent with the supreme radiance of his six arms, and whose hands on the right and left hold [objects] possessing the brilliance of the fiercely blazing flames of the fire of time (Kālānala)— [may he grant us grace].

Endowed with great power, wielding arrows, swords, bows, axes, nooses, vajras, cocks, banners, shields, ṭaṅkas, clubs, and various weapons such as khaṭvāṅgas, he is the destroyer of the Dānavas; appearing like a cloud most capable of quenching the fire of the poison emitted by the hosts of celestial beauties, he [is] the subduer of his own beauty...
...the face of the gods, beautiful with the expansion of the wheel of the power of manifest speech (*vaikharī*) that shames the pride of the body of Kandarpa (Cupid), [is] delightful; ...knowable,
born from the prowess of [his] own valor, [and] the entire ignorance of Maniravi, which is immeasurable.
Possessing eloquence manifested through the full array of the arts of knowledge,
with hands beautiful as the *vaikharī* [speech] and shining like a red lotus,
he is renowned for bestowing grace that brings prosperity to the entire world.
He whose lotus-like twelve eyes [shine forth], who is renowned for the excellence of severing the suffering of his devotees,
whose form is like that of Kārttikeya, who is the commander of the celestial army skilled in protecting the world of the gods, and who is the most excellent refuge of immeasurable majesty.
May the divine trident-staff of Śrī Subrahmaṇyaśiva’s weapon bestow meditative concentration. 11.
She who, at the time of bestowing nectar upon the entire host of gods and demons, accomplished the enchanting and beautiful subjugation of the hearts of all the oceans;
she who shines with her own form produced from the union with the illustrious Bhūtapuruṣottama Śaṅkara.

[He whose] lotus-like hands are skilled in pacifying the misfortunes wrought by various malevolent grahas such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, and vetālas; [he] who has dispelled all obstacles of the phenomenal world by means of the wonderfully variegated mudrās held [in his hands]; [and he who is attended by] Rambhā, Menakā, Tilottamā, and others...
O you whose face is the Destroyer of Death,
who are most skilled in the frantic dance (*tāṇḍava*) with feet that are alternately bent and extended, intensified at the moment of the rhythmic clapping of the hands of celestial maidens.

May the venerable Teacher, whose mount—the elephant—is surrounded by herds of female elephants delighted by the playful drinking of rut that flows from the temples of his ears; who is the instructor upon the various pedestals fashioned by the army of the Asuras; and who possesses the proximity of the divine trident-staff and the weapon of Śiva—may he grant his presence! 12.
The great central gem of the necklace that serves as a girdle for the Fortune of the three worlds; the crest-jewel of all the maidens of the Vedas; the unbroken cosmic egg.
His own mandala was adorned by a mass of rays from his hands, which resembled a cluster of white lotuses; he held two lotuses in his pair of hands...
(5th line) ...his cheeks were rendered golden-yellow by the mass of light from the jewels of his pair of earrings, and he was the thousand-colored Suparṇa... (6th line)

Shining with a body and complexion of the same hue as the sun, O Blessed Āditya, the sole eye of the world, you take your station amidst the divine trident and staff, the weapons of Śiva. Your majesty is revealed by pure rays capable of dispelling the multitude of sins that darken all the worlds; you are the ocean whose mouth is pressed down by the gods and demons.

[The city] whose beautiful stage was gladdened by the mass of the sixteen digits of the moon—trembling as it was swallowed by the garlands of flames from the terrifying, accumulated fires of the cosmic dissolution; where the various forms of Viṣṇu were distressed; where the sandalwood and *daksa* trees were flickering; and where the multitude of the sixteen digits was shimmering.

May the Moon-embodied Lord, the beloved of Rohiṇī—the divine wielder of the trident, the weapon of Śiva—whose majesty is glorified by His dwelling manifested at the tip of the matted locks of the lowest-born of the city (the skull-bearer), grant His presence with His divine trident and arrow.
24. [The divine weapons] of the trident, the discus, the arrow, the bow, and the sword... 6. [In the sky...]

His eight arms— four on the right and four on the left— are adorned with a *ṭaka*, a fresh conch, a noose, and a vajra; he possesses the majesty of an elephant in rut, and his throat is like that of a *kuṇḍa* bird, skilled in melting away the solidity of [all things] through its depth.

He whose vehicle is a lion with a deep roar and a grand onset, who is skilled in the power of crushing the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura— terrible with a burden that crushes the despondency of the enemy host— and who has spread his own majesty by devouring the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
She who acts as a lamp dispelling the mass of darkness that is the Dānavas— headed by Ṭabhadhūmṛlocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Ratnabīja, Danuja, Niśumbha, and Śambhu—
and who is adorned with various ornaments such as armlets, crowns, earrings, bracelets, girdles, waist-bands, and golden anklets.

May the goddess Śrīmurgādevī, who is white, who protects the multitude of her devoted followers, and who possesses the proximity of the divine trident and lotus—the weapons of Śiva—grant her grace. 15.
(f14a, 1st line)
May the deities of the limbs—the faces Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, along with the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapons—grant their presence.

May the five powers known as Ambikā, Gaṇāmbikā, Garvitā, Gaurī, and Umā grant their presence. May the six limb-powers known as Dharaṇi, Bhāginī, Pradyumna, Nimi, Harṣaṇī, and Praharṣaṇī grant their presence. [May] Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra...
May the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras)— Bhūmi, Svāhā, Kṣānti, Prabhā, Puṣṭi, Śruti, Kīrti, and Medhā— grant their presence to Rudra, the triple-formed one, and to Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin.

May the powers of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvara-śaktis) grant their presence. May the lords of the Gaṇas—known as Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Skanda, Devī, and Caṇḍeśvara—grant their presence. [Bhadri, Devayāni, Kundini, Kālī...]

May the powers of the eight lords of the Gaṇas— Mantrīṇī, Mālā, Āyanī, Nāmā, Āśā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Gaṇeśvarī, and Śakti— be present here. May the ten guardians of the directions, known as Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Lakṣmīśa, [also be present].
May Śacī, Svāhā, Sudarman, Dāvilāsini, Virūpā, Nidhāriṇī, Sumukhī, Nirmūlidharā, Svati, and Lakṣmī— the powers of the lords of the ten directions— be present; may they grant their presence.

May the ten weapons named the vajra, śakti, daṇḍa, khaḍga, pāśa, dhvaja, gadā, triśūla, padma, and cakra grant their presence! [Salutations] to the gracious one, to the one whose nature is the mind, to the one whose nature is the qualities, to the gentle one, to the pervasive one, to the unchanging one, and to the Great Soul.
May the other powers of the Ten-Armed One— Maṅgalātmā, Saralātmā, Capalātmā, and Nāmā— be present here.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita, Īśāna, Vijaya, Abhimāna, and Devadeva.
May Bhavodbhava, Kapālīśa, and the other eleven Rudras grant their presence; and may Vaikartana,
Vivasvat, Mārttaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Viloka, Prakāśa, Loka-sākṣin, and Trivikramāditya [grant their presence].
May the twelve Ādityas, known as Sūrya, Aṃśumat, Divākara, and the rest, be present here.
May the eight Vasus, known as Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhasa, also be present.

May they be present! May the eighteen classes of deities—the gods, sages, spirits, Daityas, Dānavas, Rudrākṣas, Māyās, serpents, Apsarases, Vidyādharas, the host of Rohiṇīs, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and Mothers—be assembled here. [May] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī [be present].
May the nine powers—Kālavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtadamani, and Manonmanī, along with Nandā and the others—be present here.
[The auspicious symbols are: the mirror, the full water-pot, the bull, the pair of chowries, the Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, and the lamp.
May these eight auspicious names grant their presence.
May they grant the presence of the auspicious. She whose side-glances, composed of auspiciousness, provide protection to the three worlds;
she who is praised by the lords of all gods and asuras.
[He] whose service is performed by all the gods— their limbs radiant with the auspicious sprouts of curiosity aroused by hearing of the excellence of his own majesty—
and who [holds] the divine trident of Śrīmat-Indrāṇī-Śiva as his foremost lotus.

May she grant her proximity! Those whose crowns are sealed by the ignorance [of worldly existence] through the touch of the lotus-feet of Dhūrjaṭi—[feet] which disregard the vessel of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) out of pride in their exceedingly powerful dūrvā-grass; and who possess the power to pulverize, dry up, and otherwise destroy the seven worlds, the seven principal mountain ranges, and the seven oceans.
Skilled in play, they are mounted upon various vehicles such as swans, bulls, peacocks, Garuḍas, buffaloes, elephants, and vultures, resplendent with their respective excellent divine weapons.
May the seven Mothers— Brahmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and the seventh named Caṇḍamuṇḍā— who shine with the beauty of full-blown lotuses,
and whose own majesty is celebrated for its capacity to endure the vastness of supreme splendor, be present here.

Seated upon a vehicle of a hideous makara, he is skilled in assuming the guise of a great cloud at the time of the world's end; his dark-blue body, possessing the luster of collyrium, completely eclipses the splendor of the sun and moon with the rays of his hands.
The splendor of her body, counted among the divine ornaments, retinues, and attendants;
she who grants the desired objects sought by all people; the form of the consort of the slayer of Madhu;
the supreme Śivā, the divine trident-weapon.
May the presence [of the deity] be established in the western petal of the lotus. [The rivers] Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Deśikā, Kauśikā, Godāvarī, Gautamī, Gomukhī,
Gaṇḍakī, Rekhā, Varuṇā, Śoṇā, Candrabhāgā, Vetravatī, Vegavatī, Kṣīra...
O divine trident,
destroyer of all weapons, may the holy rivers headed by the Kāverī and Tāmraparṇī, together with all their sacred bathing places and the serpents Ananta, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka, be present here.
May Kārkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Gulika,
Apīdhāna, and Mahānāga, together with all their hosts, manifest their presence in the gentle petal of the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon,
arising from the fourteen worlds.

The Supreme Lord, consecrated by the imperial coronation (paṭṭābhiṣeka), who possesses the authority to bestow the fruits of the ritual procedures for Śiva-worship performed with lotus-like hands by the entire multitude of devotees of Śiva— including gods, demons, madanagandharvas, siddhas, sāddhyas, vidyādharas, daityas, brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others.

One whose mental activity is perpetually restrained by the meditation upon the pair of his own lotus feet, which are an uninterrupted blue [in color], and who is honored by tens of millions of the lords of Śiva’s hosts.

May Caṇḍeśvara— the possessor of greatness and countless meritorious deeds, the fierce sun capable of shattering the mass of darkness that is the sins of those bowing at his lotus feet, and the presence within the divine trident-lotus of Śiva’s weapon— grant his grace.
O lotus-eyed one, whose beautiful filaments possess the splendor of a multitude of clouds hanging in the sky entwined with the *śambara* plant,
and who is accompanied by the wielder of the skull-topped trident (*kāpāla-śūla*) raised by his lotus-like hand; O you who are seated upon the lotus of Brahmā!
His neck shone, adorned with a garland of skulls, a necklace, and armlets; his cheeks were honored by the red flowers, saffron, and parched grain offered by his devotees;
[he partook of] milk-rice, sugar-rice, and mung-bean rice.
He who delights in offerings of rice, black gram cakes, and various types of sweetmeats and betel; he who has utterly destroyed the lineage of the Daityas with his fierce and terrifying roar;
he whose face is formidable with a barking and powerful dog capable of threatening wicked people and enemies; and he whose vehicle is the son of the Earth (Bhīma).
The expert in subduing the entire host of obstacles, his circle of matted locks tawny with a mass of radiance like that of the rising sun, the naked youth,
and the dark-bodied Guru.
May Mahābhairava, surrounded by the eight Bhairavas known as Aṭṭahāsa, Caṇḍakrodha, Matta, Kṛtānta, Kapālin, Bhīṣaṇa, Saṃhāra, and Paritakṣetrapāla,
manifest his presence near the divine trident of Śiva’s weapon.
[O you who are] honored by gods, asuras, the best of sages, siddhas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, garuḍas, gāndharvas, kiṃnaras, kimpuruṣas, bhūtas, pretas,
piśācas, siddhayoginīs, śākinīs, and brahmarākṣasas; [O you whose] eyes are fierce with white passion, [and who are surrounded by] men and deer...

[The worlds] of birds, stationary and moving beings, the earth-world (*bhūrloka*), the intermediate space-world (*bhuvarloka*), the heaven-world (*suvarloka*), the great heaven-world (*maharloka*), the heat-world (*tapoloka*), the truth-world (*satyaloka*), the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the egg of Garuḍa, the egg of Viṣṇu, the egg of Rudra, the egg of the Bull, the interior of the egg, the exterior of the egg, and the seven eggs.
The seven netherworlds—Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Sutala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Talātala, and Pātāla;
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Ārkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Gulika, and Aṣṭa, the eight great nāgas; Mount Mahāmeru, Mount Himavat, and Mount Krauñca.
The Sunrise Mountain, the Niṣadha Mountain, the Malaya Mountain, the Mandara Mountain, the Vindhya Mountain, Mount Kailāsa, and other such mountains;
the seven oceans known as the Salt, Sugarcane, Wine, Butter, Curd, Milk, and Sweet waters; and the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sindhu rivers.
Sarasvatī, Gautamī, Godāvarī, Kāverī, Śoṇa, Nandī, Āsava, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Ākāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Bhṛgu, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Yājñavalkya.

Nārada, the nine planets, the ten guardians of the directions, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, the three Ṛbhus, and the thirty-three crores of Gaṇas; the Lord of the fourteen worlds, the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the mantras of five syllables, six syllables, eight syllables, nine syllables, ten syllables, and the sixteen vowels, as well as the Great Mantra and the syllable *huṃ*.

The utterances *phaṭ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *namaḥ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*; pleasure and pain; the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*); the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the elements, and the sense organs; and speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals, as well as speaking, walking, grasping, excretion, and procreation.

The bliss of emission (*visargānanda*), sound, touch, form, taste, smell, hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna* [breaths], as well as the *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkala*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* [winds], and the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, *suṣumnā*, *gandhārī*, and *hastijihvā* [nadīs].
The tongue, the lap, the Puṣā, the Yaśasvinī, the Kuhu,
and the Śaṅkhinī; the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Ājñā, Bālātapā, Brahmaraṃdhra, and Hālā.

[The work] which destroys the poison of falsehood, [reveals] the nectar of the manifold reality of all things— both visible and invisible, prose and verse— [and subdues] the Vaiśeṣikas, Naiyāyikas, Lokāyatas, Mīmāṃsakas, Cārvākas, and Cāraṇas;

it is the royal swan among the words of the Bharatas, the resting place for those who maintain the truth, and the ultimate kalpa-sūtra that resolves the eighteenfold doubts regarding the Smṛtis, Śrutis, words, forms, and so forth.
Śrīkaṇṭha, who is honored by the Śaiva Āgamas and is proficient in the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Tarkaśāstras, the Nītiśāstras, and the Bhaktijana-muni-prabhāva [treatises] of Pārvatī;
he is the bearer of the Gaṅgā of eternal bliss and eternal auspiciousness.
O Leader of the Gaṇas, O Three-eyed One, Lord of the Three Worlds, together with the illustrious Kāmākṣī—
[this is] the supreme [devotion] for the service of the auspicious festival at the end of the holy site of the thirteen-day flag-hoisting of the glorious and venerable Ekāmranātha.
By the command of the Lord of the Earth, all the deities assembled there; and by the order of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkara’s army, [the sounds of] mṛdaṅgas,
lutes, flutes, cymbals, tālakas, kāhalas, kettledrums, mardalas, conchs, paṭahas, and eighteen kinds of musical instruments resounded here.
I shall provide a summary.
(Third Line) We know the one with three peaks; we meditate upon the one whose feet are the Vedas. May that Bull inspire us.
(4th line) Having spoken thus, one should hoist the cloth; having joined the cord into a single strand, one should bind it in a clockwise direction.

Afterwards, one should join the eight lords of the vidyās— Kambha, Nidhi, Dhvaja, Daṇḍa, and the others— at the tips of the petals in the order starting from the south, and then consecrate them. Afterwards...

Having worshipped Vṛṣabheśvara with all the offerings, such as food offerings (naivedya), incense, lamps, and so forth, one should offer oblations (bali) with the mantra "Oṃ [Name] Svāhā" at the tips of the petals in the directions to the eight Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Ukṣā, and present an offering consisting of coconut, plantain, betel nut, betel leaf, and betel, along with incense and lamps.
After giving [the offering], one should then offer a blessing:
"Salutations to the illustrious Ekāmbanātha, accompanied by the illustrious Kāmākṣyambā. The invocation of the deity is complete. May there be auspiciousness, auspiciousness!

[I bow to] the one with the face of the best of elephants, the son of the Daughter of the Mountain, the friend of the Gaṇas, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Master who holds an axe in his trunk-like hand, whose hands are adorned with bracelets, and who has swallowed a lotus.
This *Ṣaḍgarittāla* is to be praised by the best of gods, spoken by the beautiful Sundara, held with ease, and saluted by the deities; it reveals the *Tāla* measure,
possesses the color of the excellent elephant-faced Lord (Gaṇeśa),
bears the hue of Śiva’s saffron, is adorned by white conch-shells and serpents, and bestows blessings upon Mālava.

I praise Gaṇapati, the Lord who is adorned by the rays of the jewels on the hoods of the serpents that serve as the ornaments for his three eyes; whose body is whitened, who has shattered delusion, who is praised by Hari, Hara, and the gods, and who is the rhythm (tāla) of Gaṇapati— the Rāga Gaṇapatitāla.
Let him cause the dance of the pure forest-rows,
the song of the cloud-like petals, and the music of the drums with the five great sounds to resound.
I pay homage to the Bull-like God, who possesses a white complexion and a beautiful form.
To him who possesses sharp, beautiful, and lofty horns; to him whose feet are the Vedas; to the one who bestows bliss.
The vehicle of Śambhu,

white as the moon and the kunda flower, is properly praised by the mouths of the gods beginning with Śailādi; it is always attended by the faces of the inhabitants of heaven and possesses a deep resonance.

I bow to the one who bestows the earth, including the worlds and their foundations; to the protector of cows and others, the supreme bestower of liberation; to the giver of Dharma, the joyful one. (4th line) He whose pair of lotus-feet are perpetually bowed to by all the gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, siddhas, vidyādharas, bhūtas, vetālas, and so forth; he who is the boon-granter of Śambhu, upon whose face the orb of the young sun rests like a lotus. (5th–6th lines)

Dāvāhana, whose very nature is the Dharma of Vinita, possesses four feet consisting of the Vedas; he has filled the quarters of the sky with masses of golden dust rising from his firmly established hooves, which have turned them tawny; on the tips of his massive horns are fixed a multitude of large wicks and other ornaments; he is the Lord of Bulls, pervading the intermediate space.

Together with the first group of his own attendants dwelling in the regions of the earth and the netherworld (pātāla), [this work is dedicated] to the venerable Śrīmad-Ekāmranātha, who is accompanied by Ambā Kāmākṣī; he is the Supreme Lord whose sport is Pārvatī, and who effects the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of the entire universe, acting under the command of the Supreme Lord Bhagavān.
On the thirteenth day,

for the purpose of serving the auspicious occasion at the conclusion of the flag-hoisting festival at Tīrthānta, Nandikeśvara, surrounded by his own retinue, arrived, fulfilling the command of the Supreme Lord.

Sacrificing with a bull and clarified butter, they have overcome all adversaries; by means of this bull, they have driven away the attacking armies. For him whose bull is being led forth as an oblation for Indra, he drives back the approaching enemy. Oṃ Hāṃ.
Salutation to the one whose seat is the bull; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the form of the bull.
The bull has the form of a bull, possesses three eyes, and his mind is solely intent upon Rudra;
he is the very embodiment of Dharma and is as pure and stainless as a clear crystal.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Bull; with "vṛṣabhāya svāhā," I offer this oblation. This Bull, possessing the auspicious form of the best of mountains, who has become the vehicle of Śiva—him, the tranquil, the infinite, the dust-free, firm in his exertion, whose gait is steady, and whose limbs are as beautiful as those of a rutting elephant.
Her body was kissed by the bees as they wandered about, her feet were tawny like fragrant lotuses, and she wore a beautiful bodice that resounded with the tinkling of swaying clusters of jewels,
while the dance of the celestial nymphs arose in harmony with the melody of her song.

O Lord of the Earth, may there be victory, victory! O you who possess the axe that grants the boon of true devotion; O you whose feet, like lotuses, are the resting place for the rays of the sun; O you who are the bull among kings, the rhythm of the *tāla* is the bull itself, and the melody is the dance of the noble elephant at twilight.

There is dancing, leaf-clappers, and other instruments; there is the music of the *kubhava* drum— by the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkarasena, I cause a great clamor with mṛdaṅgas, lutes, flutes, *phaṇava*, cymbals, *kāhala*, conchs, kettledrums, and the sounding of large drums.
(3rd line) Salutations to you, the Lord of the World; salutations to you, the Creator; salutations to you whose form is the Veda; salutations to you, O Brahman. To the glorious Vattāravinda...
(4th line)

To the bee-like [devotee] who is drenched by the continuous flow of the honey of the *timiga* fruit, [I offer] salutations to the Lord who is the sole abode of Dharma in the form of a tortoise, and whose banner bears a swan on a wing [emerging] from the Himalayas— the source of the Gaṅgā; salutations made by those who have bowed down to Śiva, the protector of living beings, for the sake of his beloved consort Bhāṣā.
To this Brahmā, whose form is entirely composed of the syllable *Om*, who is of the color of gold, who possesses three eyes, and who is like the Vedas themselves—
we offer salutations. He holds a lotus, a water-pot, and a rosary in his left hands, while in his right hands he holds a staff and a goad, and he is accompanied by Hāsa and Śri.

(Third line) Having assumed a body grown with matted locks by the command of the Lord of Gods, and having served [him], let him come quickly to celebrate the festival of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva). (Fourth line) Let he whose face, arms, and feet are [marked]... arrive.
In which the four castes were fully developed; which was the first to bring forth [the path];
and which was perfected through the eight limbs produced by the yoga of posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption.

He is renowned for having attained the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, drawn forth by his distinguished yoga; he whose four faces are the reservoirs of the nectar of all the Vedas; he who dwells in the world of Satyaloka, which is free from death and unsurpassed; and he who, through the union with Sarasvatī, has assumed the form of his beloved.

His golden body is adorned with beautiful chowries fluttering like tender sprouts, and with a pure lotus-girdle swinging like a necklace; he possesses a luster that dispels darkness, whose nature is pure knowledge, who holds a lotus as his weapon while seated in the lotus posture, and whose feet are equal in hue to the *vakula* flower, following the rhythm of the *brahmatāla*.
Brahmā, who is fond of his own five-colored lotus-seat, whose central direction is protected by the command of the Supreme Lord,
[is endowed with] the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan Vedas, the Śāstras, the eighteen Purāṇas, and the Smṛtis.

And those who are the embodiments of all mantras, headed by the seventy million great mantras that name the deities of the sixty-four arts beginning with [the aforementioned], such as Kauśika, Kāśyapa, and Bhāradvāja.

Jagadguru Āgastya by name, the primordial teacher, and the hosts of sages; and Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Satyaka, Mahendra, Āditya, Bhṛśa, Antarikṣa, Agni, Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, the planets, Kṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhaṅgarāja, Nirṛti, Dauḥsvāruka, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Pracetā.
Tā, Sura, Śoṣa, Roga, Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Phalla, Aṭaka, Saumya, Mṛgāditi, Aditi, Āpāpavatsa, Savitra,
Savitra, Indu, Indrajit.
Rudra, Rudradāsa, Kāmarīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, Dharādhara, Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, the sinful Rākṣasī, Skanda, Aryaman,
Ajaṅgabali, Piñchābhidāna, and all the tutelary deities, as well as Viṣṇu and his attendants, [dwelling] in the divine and intermediate realms.
And all the hosts of Brahmās dwelling on the surface of the earth and in the netherworlds (pātāla),
O Pārvatī, [are subject] to the Blessed Lord Parameśvara, who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of these thousand-fold worlds.
For the amusement of his play, accompanied by his mother,

for the sake of the prosperity of the Lord of the Earth, on the thirteenth day, for the purpose of performing the auspicious rites of ascending the banner at the holy site, [he] fulfilled the command of the Supreme Lord.
That central region, surrounded by the assembly of Brahmā’s own hosts, was gathered together.

"Brahma, born of the spirit, arose first in the east... (4th line)... from the two boundaries, with divine splendor; his highest forms, reaching to the depths, were those of the existent and the non-existent.
The seat of the non-existent, Oṃ Hāṃ (5th line), salutation to the seat of Brahmā; salutation to the form of Brahmā.
Brahmā is four-faced, yellow in color, and adorned with a staff in each of his four hands.

[He who is] endowed with a sacrificial ladle, staff, and *akṣamālā* (rosary), wearing a crown, and having the swan as his vehicle— Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā; Oṃ Svāhā, I offer this oblation (*bali*) to Brahmā,
the lover of the lotus, the lotus-born.

Obeisance to the one who is the cause of the cause of the supreme beloved, whose lotus-like eyes rest upon the four-faced one, who is more beautiful than the interior of the lotus, the beloved of the beautiful one, and the one for whom song and dance are dear; to Hiraṇyagarbha, the Grandfather, whose sound is like that of the bherī, maddala, murava, dholli, and conch, and who is remembered as Brahmā, whose song and dance are continuous and measured by the *tāla* beat.

O Śaṅkarasena, lord of the army, [these are] the *tāla* called *brahmatāla*, the *rāga* called *vakularāha*, the dance called *sampāda*, the fifth-note melody (*pañcama*) called *parṇa*, and the instrumental music (*vādya*) called *cañcapuṭa*.

"By the command of Caṇḍeśvara, with mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, flutes, cymbals, tālakas, kāhalas, conchs, and paṭaha drums, I shall here sound the great drum (bherī) and the saṅkhoṣaṇa. Thus ends the Brahma-sandhi.
Salutations to the lord of the best of gods, the granter of boons, the illustrious Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand, the thousand-eyed one, the wise one;

whose pride was quelled by ascending the shoulders of Airāvata—white as jasmine, sandalwood, nectar, and snow—and lofty with tusks like the moon; who brings satisfaction to the gods who bow before him, and who received Gautama in a firm embrace.

We worship the beloved one with full, beautiful, and lovely breasts; the one who surpassed the gods in play; the one whose feet are worthy of worship by Mahendra; the one with a body dark as a blue lotus; the one who holds a thunderbolt in his two arms; the one mounted upon the elephant-vehicle; and the son of Śacī, surrounded by gods and lords of sages.

Accompanied by the sound of kettledrums, dancing, and song, Indra, the lord of the gods, arrived at the festival of Giriśa at the command of the Lord of Gods; he was surrounded by the thirty deities, and his [chariot] was rendered doubly crimson by the gems set in the crowns of all the gods and goddesses.
The sprout-like feet [of the Lord],
whose form is like a thousand-petaled lotus born from the waters of the nectar of his own body’s exquisite beauty, are like the Pārijāta tree brought from the Nandana grove by the Thousand-eyed One.

His limbs were enchanting, adorned with garlands of flowers; his own body was being fanned by the proud female pigeons dwelling upon the roof-terraces of the celestial chariots borne by a thousand steeds of Indra;
and his chest was made beautiful by the spreading fragrance of saffron and sandalwood from the breasts of Śacī, who dwells in the city of Amarāvatī.
With a trunk fierce in its agitation like the churning of the lotus-thicket of the Asura army, his hard palm was used for rubbing the slopes of Airāvaṇa’s frontal globes;
he possessed a sharp hundred-edged blade for the execution of the haughty enemies of the gods.

With his staff-like arms adorned, he is fond of the *carcapuṭa* scale and the notes of the *saṅgīta*, *samatāla*, *bhairavī*, *bhujaṅga*, and *nṛtta* rhythms performed together with the entire assembly of gods led by Urvaśī; he is the one who protects the eastern quarter in accordance with the command of the Supreme Lord.
Indra, the seven worlds known as Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Suvarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka; and Vaikartana,
Viśvasvat, Ārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśa, Loka-sākṣin, and Trivikramāditya.

The twelve [zodiacal signs] beginning with Aries, known as the Sun and so forth; the nine planets named the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu; and the twenty-eight lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Revatī.
[Together with] the twenty-seven lunar mansions up to Revatī, and [the goddesses] beginning with Urvaśī, Gaṇeśī, Sukeśī, Kāmukī, Kāmavardhanī,
Pījanī, Nīlambinī, Sumukhī, Vikṛti, Viśvarūpī, Vegavatī, Ākrāntā, Pakṣapātinī, Tilottamā, Śobhā, Bhadrā, Vidyā, Mañjughoṣaṇā, and others.

[He saw] the deities presiding over the ages— Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— as well as the Apsarases, and the deities presiding over the moments, lava-s, nimiṣas, kāṣṭhās, kalās, muhūrtas, yāmas, days and nights, fortnights, months, and solstices.

And the presiding deities of the seasons, years, yugas, kalpas, manvantaras, pralayas, and mahāpralayakalpas; and all the hosts of Indras dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld (pātāla)— together with these, [he is the cause] of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire universe, of the Blessed One.
The eastern Indra, who has fulfilled the command of the Supreme Lord, has arrived surrounded by his own hosts; he is the protector, the deliverer, and the one invoked in every call for aid.
I invoke the heroic Indra, the one invoked by many; may Indra, the protector of the sacrifice, grant us well-being. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Indra;
obeisance to the form of Indra.
One should visualize [Indra] mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, golden-hued, wearing a diadem,
possessing a thousand eyes, holding a discus, and with the thunderbolt in his hand.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra; "svāhā to Indra," with these words I offer the bali. In the eastern direction, [I offer it] to the one who is the bird upon the sprout of reality, which has blossomed through the destruction of the host of gods.
From the great hand of Hanaspraha, before the great sound of Indra in the city of the quarters, he directed the auspicious forest in front of Indra.
(4th line) The *tāla* was *samatāla*, the *rāga* was *Bhairavī*; there was the dance of the serpent, the dance of Parṇakāmeśa, the *ghidya*, and the *capuṭa*.
(5th line) Thus [ends the work] of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkara’s army.

"By command, I shall cause a proclamation with the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, flutes, paṇavas, āḍambaras, conchs, kahalas, śaṅkhas, paṭahas, ahaha-drums, and bherīs. Thus ends the section on Indra's alliance.

Salutations to Agni, who has the form of Rudra, and to Vaiśvānara; salutations to that Śiva, whose nature is the dissolution of all things, and who is the source of fear for the world— this homage is to you.

To him who is ever-victorious, the pervasive one with seven flames, whose body has become the manifest form of the Lord himself, whose banner is the goat leaping upon a ram—may he protect me for even a moment. For without him, this entire world, consisting of all moving and non-moving beings from the consumer of oblations to the flesh-eater, would perish;
he whose face shines like the red body of fire.

With seven tongues and a jaw that bears a mass of flaming nets, the Lord is mounted upon the form of a ram; He is joined with Svāhā and other Śaktis, holding a golden lotus, a spear, and a club, and is accompanied by Māra and the Nāgas.

The assembly of the Śikhins has gathered; he whose birth was consecrated by the lotus-hands of the four Śaṅkaras, whose power consists in the capacity to bestow the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* that satisfy the entire host of gods, asuras, and ancestors, who dwells in the city of Tejovatī, and who performs all sacrificial rites— [he has arrived].
The cause,
consisting of compassion, O Goddess Svāhā, beloved of the Lord, eternally mounted upon a red ram, the destroyer of the evils of all worlds...
O Great Power, whose form consists of light blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction; you who are joined with the delightful sound of the rhythmic clapping of intoxicated celestial damsels;
you who are beloved by the Lord of Kaulīs through your exquisite dancing; and you who are protected by the command of the Supreme Lord in the southeastern quarter.
Agni, Agastya, Pulastya, Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra,
Kauśika, Kukṣa... Valmīka, Vāmadeva,
Vaiśampāyana, Tumburu, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Citrasena, Kapila, Kaṇva, and Kāśya.
Pāntī, Rogaita, Māgastya, Garva, Gālava, Vācyāyana, Jamadagni, Jagadguru, Jābāli, Dadhīci,
Devala, Dūrvāsas, Nārada, Parāśara, Bādarāyaṇa, Bhṛgu, Bhāradvāja, Marīci, Romaharṣaṇa, Mārkaṇḍeya, Yājñavalkya, Rudra, and Kauṇḍinya.
May the entire host of seers, including Nyaśa, Auśanaka, Śuka, Harita, and others,
together with their wives and sons, and all these [deities], along with Agni— the lord of the southeastern quarter who creates the entire world— surrounded by his own retinue, come hither.

O Agni, you who are ruddy and pervasive, being wise, ward off the wrath of the god; protect us through the sacrificial formula, O most excellent one, for our nourishment; shine forth, O all-encompassing one, and drive away those who hate us.

Be gracious to us. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Agni; salutation to the root-mantra. [I worship] him who bears the seven-flamed fire, holding a rosary and a water-pot, adorned with garlands of flames, with a lotus in his hand and a spear in his other hand, seated upon a goat. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agni. With "jyaṃ agnaye svāhā," I offer this oblation.

Red, delighting in red, the eye red from grasping the peak of the crow; red, the crown of matted hair born of delight, with the sounds *ḍama-ḍama* and *kṛ-kṛ*; *gam-gam*, *tuṅga-mndha*, *nandha-rimal-mida*; this is the protection against the seizing demon.
The embryo, the hip, the head, and the crab;
increasing, increasing, the burning inflicted by the thunderbolt and Yama; *haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ*, *kricita kricita*; may the qualities of the gods [be] upon the shore of the flood... that very thing.
On the rugged slopes of the Krama mountain, there is the *tālamattā* rhythm, the *varāli* melody, the *nṛtta* dance, the *maṇḍala* formation, and the *parṇaka-asthi-vādya* instrument;
thus, I shall cause the drum of Śaṅkarasena, the commander-in-chief, to resound— this is the "Fire-junction" (*agnisandhi*).
(4th line) Homage to you, O Dharmarāja, and homage to Vivasvat; homage to Yama, the god, and homage to the witness of the worlds. Puṇyā... (5th line) puṇya.

I ever salute the beloved of the crescent-moon, who grants fearlessness through his own will and fear through his will, whose weapon is the staff of formidable punishment, who is adorned with earrings, whose vehicle is a buffalo that moves restlessly among various ghosts and spirits, whose banner is beautiful with garlands, and who is self-controlled at the end of time.

When the Lord of Devas, whose body is in the center, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a banner, a noose, and a staff, with a cruel gaze and eyes like the fire at the end of time, wielding the staff known as Kāla, accompanied by hosts of Bhūtas and Pretas— [he is] the Sovereign of the Gods.
By the one to be known, who is to be purified by the fires of the highest [wisdom], and who has most swiftly attained union with the Daughter of the Sun—
who illuminates the twenty-four abodes of the universe and possesses manifold forms— [there arose] Mukunda, Śatānanda, and other tigers among the gods.
The heat [of the world], which bestows the fruits of black and white karma upon the upward and downward migrations, is the path that restrains the weary mind;

it is the witness to the entire multitude of moving and unmoving beings dwelling within the stages [of existence], and it is terrifying with tusks sharpened by the thunderbolt-like [force] of the great mountains shaken by one’s own breath.

(6th line) He whose vehicle is the buffalo, who wields a fierce staff capable of crushing the lineage of the thorns of the world, [and] who is the elephant of the god of love joined with the palm-clapping of Bhṛṅgiṇī—
(f33a, 1st line)

[He] who is dear to the sound of the lute, who is protected by the command of the Supreme Lord, [and] whose southern quarter is guarded by Yama; and the seven Mothers— Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā— as well as the protectors beginning with Virabhadra and Vighneśvara, [possessing] the power of hearing, memory, intelligence, and wisdom.

Śānti, Raudri, Nāma, Brahmā, and the Mothers; the Protectors from Agni and Prajāpati onwards; O Vāgīśvarī, [the goddesses] Kriyā, Kartṛ, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Vidya, Kānti, Śaśi, Bhūmi, and Narmadā; the Mothers; the Protectors from Śrīdara and Nṛsiṃha onwards; and Jayin, Vijayin, Jayantī, and Vijṛmbhitā.
Bhiṇya, Parājivira,
Bhadrakālī, the Maruts, the Mothers, and the Pālakas as far as Śūkra and Gaṇḍharva; [and] the protectors of the sky, the intermediate space, and the earth, according to the ritual injunctions...
The three classes of [deities], as well as the Yoginīs and Ḍākinīs, those named Vairāja, Barhiṣat, Niṣpānta, Mūrti, and Bahudhanya;
the Pitṛ-gaṇas, those named Kalottaka, Vṛkodara, and Citragupta; and the Yamapāṣṇi-gaṇas from the celestial, atmospheric, terrestrial, and the nether regions of Pātāla.
And the hosts of Vasīs, Sanaīścara, and Yama— these, together with him,
having been commanded by the Supreme Lord to perform the creation of the entire world,
arrived at the four crossroads, surrounded by their own retinues, and granted fearlessness to all beings.
In which constellation he was born, O King... in which the gods consecrated him—let us worship that Citragu of his with an oblation. Om Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Yama;
obeisance to the embodied form.

One should meditate upon Kṛtānta, the lord of the southern direction—mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in his hand, terrifying, bearing the noose of Time (*kālapāśa*), and black in color—with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*. I offer this oblation (*bali*) with the mantra: *jyaṃ yamāya svāhā*. [The remainder of the verse is: *sārisārisurasannibha-sārisārisalilaṃ kakāsannibhaka...*
(f34.a 1st line) The night-stalker [Rāvaṇa] brandished his exceedingly sharp sword, which resembled the peak of Mount Madagiri; that Mount Madagiri peak...
(2nd line)

With a most sharp sword, with the rhythmic clapping of palms like falling palm-fruits, with the dance of the *rāga* of the Khurjara, with the staff-like foot, with the leaf-robe of Kauśika, and with the three-fold purity of speech—
thus do I proclaim the sounding of the drum for the commander Śaṅkarasena; this is the Yamasaṃdhi...
Salutations to the devotee of Śaṅkara; salutations to you, the lord of the Daityas.

Salutations to you, the lord of the Rākṣasas, the great Nirṛti. Salutations eternally to the one who is surrounded by Vetālas, Bhūtas, and others, whose hair is the blazing, flickering fire, and whose surface is the netherworld (atala).
I bow to the one whose form is like a yellow egg, who destroys those devoid of faith,
who is a worshiper of the lotus feet of Paśupati, the protector of the lowly, and whose excellent eyes are red with compassion; he who wields the trident as his weapon against all enemies of heaven.
With blood-red eyes, clad in garments dyed crimson by the host of demons, dark blue in hue, wielding a sword and a shield, equipped with various weapons, and mounted upon a lion-vehicle—
his cavernous mouth intent on biting with fangs, accompanied by great Rākṣasas bearing maces— may Nirṛti swiftly arrive for the festival of Giriśa.

...the righteous people, who have increased their endurance through the harsh discipline of great courage, intent on bestowing the fear of birth, death, and old age upon those defiled by the stains of the four impurities; (4th line)... [endowed with] patience.
He who performs prostrations with devotion toward Śiva—the one who subdued the hosts of swift-moving night-stalkers intent on destroying the Dharma; who resides in the city of Kṛṣṇāvatī;
and who is exalted by his fleet-footedness that traverses the entire universe.
Lāvāhana, whose palms were scarred by the striking of his formidable sword which resembled the smoke from the breath of the Lord of Serpents;
who was fond of the *naṭṭa* musical mode, terrifying due to the dangling serpents on his armlets; and who was the right hand of the Supreme Lord, protected by His command.
In the western month [are the names of] Niriti, Namuci, the Daityas, Indumukunda, Sukunda, Surāri, Suloma, Mahājṛmbha, Śaṅkukarṇa...
[Hayaśrīva], Hālāhala, Kākadeha, Kākapāda, Balābala, Calācala, Niṣkalāvidhāna, Mai... [and others].

...with testicles shaped like jars, a belly shaped like a water-pot, two faces, a buffalo face, a boar face, and a lion face; [the one] with golden hair, the Great Time (Mahākāla), the navel of Brahmā, the tusk of Brahmā, [the one] like a small cave-fortress, the one with a beautiful face, the foremost Bhairava, and the Dwarf (Vāmana).

The hosts of spirits known as Mahāvīra, Vīreśvara, Śaṅkhapāla, Gulikādra, and Aṣṭākṣa— those whose hunger is unveiled, whose tongues are long, and who are fleshless, blood-drinking, victorious, swift, and devoid of fear.

And the hosts of pretas named Nirāmayana, as well as Lohitākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Viśālākṣa, Bhīṣaṇa, Abhimada, Daṃṣṭrogra, Dāma, Mahodara, Mahākāya, Siṃhajvālāsya, Mānavāmanaka, Ambukalaṅbuka, Krūravegī, Rihāra, Śrottuṅga, Kumbhakarṇa, Pūrṇodara, and Vakralocana.
(3rd line) And the hosts of Rākṣasas, such as Guṇautkaṭa, Piśitāśana, Ṛddhi, and Kārādi, who dwell in the divine realms, the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworlds of Pātāla; (4th line)

And all the hosts of Nirṛti, together with these, having been commanded by the Supreme Lord for the creation of the entire world, arrived at the western quarter. Surrounded by his own host, Nirṛti approached from the four directions, saying: "Seek out him who does not press the Soma and does not sacrifice; seek out the thief among men; [seek] another for us."
Sādāyityā! Homage, O Goddess Nirṛti; may it be unto you! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of Nirṛti; homage to Mūkti!
The Lord of Rākṣasas has blood-red eyes, is mounted upon a corpse, possesses the luster of a blue lotus petal, holds a sword in his hand... [and] drinks the sky. Oṃ hāṃ.

(Second line) *Namaḥ* to Nirṛti; *svāhā* to Nirṛti, I offer this oblation (*bali*). O you who possess eyes agitated by the destruction of the *rakṣas*, the *karaka*, the *maṇika*, the *kakṣa*, and the *kṣaya*.
(Third line) [O you whose] momentary glance [is directed toward them].

Possessing a playful brilliance, swiftly cutting down the hosts of enemy elephants with his hands, bearing that most excellent of weapons which destroys the darkness of the Kali age, he— whose hair is dark blue like a sapphire— performs the sacrifice of battle, manifesting his prowess as he whirls about.
At this very time, in the midst of the great conflagration that consumes all things, amidst the fierce flames, with the sound of the *tālamalla* drum,

the *rāgabhairavī* dance that terrifies the serpents, and the music of the *parṇanaṭṭa* and *bhāṣa* instruments along with the *kaṃbuka* shell, I, [the one] presiding over the vegetable broth, sound the proclamation upon the kettle-drum.

Thus ends the section on Nirṛti. (3rd line) Homage, homage to you, Varuṇa, the son of Pracetā, who holds the noose for seizing in his hand; homage, homage to you who have destroyed the host of obstacles. (4th line)
[He who] created the variegated world, whose weapon is the noose, the roar of the hunter, the supreme treasury of awakening, the slayer of the enemy, [whose path is] the sound of the wheel...
singing, the jewel of fear, the beauty of grace.

Surrounded by the limbs of sporting women like the celestial elephant Airāvata, he was like the sky encircled by the sun; he bore the command of Hara, and the shark-bannered god (Varuṇa) had ascended [him],
resembling a jasmine flower, the moon, or a conch shell, adorned with armlets.
Together with the gods, their hearts filled with joy, amidst the sounds of drums, dancing, and singing, they longed to serve his command after a long time.
For the festival of the mountain, Varuṇa quickly arrived; [he who is] the supreme person, the refuge from the cycle of worldly existence, and the supreme purifier of committed sins.
Surrounded by a circle of great sages such as Rāmaśuddha, Catuḥsarasvatī, Marṣaṇa, and Mārkaṇḍeya; the moon upon the head of Śaṅkara,
whose rays are like a stream of nectar that revives the entire multitude of the gods of speech.

Skilled in guarding the treasury of the entire heap of fresh jewels; possessing a four-square movement upon the crest of the continuous waves of the ocean of Sagara, which dwells in Sarasvatīpura within the realm of Aśeṣa...; whose vehicle is the Makara.

The Gaṅgā, whose dark-blue belly contains the ocean; who holds in her hand the skillful noose drawn forth from the entire host of wicked Dānavas; who is beloved by the gods of the peaks of the Navatāla and Siṃhatāla mountains; and who protects the western region below as commanded by the Supreme Lord.
Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Godāvarī, Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī, Kanyā, Payoṣṇī, Sarayū, Tāmraparṇī, Gaṅgā, and Gandhavatī.

The seven oceans, distinguished by the names of salt, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sweet water, headed by the great Nandī and all the daughters of the Tīrthaṅkaras; and the seven netherworlds (pātālas), known by the names Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Sutala, Mahātala, Sātalā, and Talātala.
(5th line) Nica, Kṛtu, Dakṣa, Kāla, Kārmaka, Vasu, Satya, Dhara, Rucira, Pūru, or Śobhi by name— the Viśvedevas— and Caṇḍaru—
(f38.a 1st line)
The Viśvedevas— namely Drāma, Mahāvega, Vibudha, Piṅgala, Ūtāma, Viśvarūpa, Viśālākṣa, Bhūdhara, Mekhala, and Vāhana—
as well as all the hosts of Varuṇa residing in the heavens, the intermediate space, the earth, Pātāla, and Atala; together with these, [is] the creation and maintenance of the entire world.
(Third line) In the western quarter, during the withdrawal [of the world], Varuṇa, surrounded by his own host, having arrived at the fourfold expanse, is being saluted by Brahmā.
(Fourth line)
One should meditate upon Varuṇa, whose body is radiant and white as the moon, seated upon a crocodile. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa; jya, svāhā to Varuṇa.

(Fifth line) I offer this oblation. [He who is] difficult to overcome due to his formidable form, with conch-like mounds blossoming on the slopes of his hips, possessing a beautiful and graceful body... [he is] Varuṇa.
His shoulders are marked by the lotus-like feet of the Goddess, his chest is adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments, and he is accompanied by the gods and the enemies of the gods.
The *nesijagarva*, the *karatalalola-sindhuvihāra*, the *tāla* (third line), the *navatāla*,
the *rāga*, the *deśika*, the *nṛtta*, the *kuñcita*, the *parṇaśrīkāma*, the *vādya*, and the *sihmānanda*— thus [ends] the *Śaṅkarasenā*. (fourth line)
"I shall cause the sound of the drum to resound"—
this is the Varuṇa-sandhi.
(5th line)

Salutations to you who have the deer as your seat; salutations to you who bear the goad; salutations to you, the wind-god among the gods; salutations to you, Vāyu. I bow to the slayer of the Gandharvas...
whose body is composed of the essence of the elephant and the swan, who eternally sustains the multitude of all living beings, and who perfectly originates from the deer and the horse.
...the protector of the entire triple world, beginning with Indra and Pitāmaha; upon which limbs [is he situated]?

Within which [limbs] does he dwell? He who is surrounded by Nanda and others, adorned with the deer-vehicle, the banner, the *jaya*, the *rodāma*, and so forth, and accompanied by the smoke-colored Maruts...
Accompanied by the rivers and joined with the Goddess Śakti,
the vital breath— present in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, the life-force of the six worlds,
worshipped by the lords of men— is exceedingly fit for the festival of Giriśa; thus the wind has arrived as the fourth.

The multitude of living beings is pervaded by the five vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*; he bears the burden of the seven worlds, which are supported by the seven pillars of the *āvāhana* and other rites; and he is protected by the rules of the thousandfold *śikṣā*.
Renowned as Vītihotra Maitra, he is one who takes pity upon all people through the internal signs manifested by his hands; he acts with the signs of intention, touch, and fearlessness;
he dwells in the city of Ga...; he strikes terror into the divine armies; and his weapons and banners are raised high.
Accompanied by Balitāla, with his crown adorned by a serpent, beloved by the sound of the mountain-dwelling Keśin, surrounded by the command of the Supreme Lord,
he is the Wind-god of the north-western quarter;
[he is] Kālī, Karālikā, Labhadrikā, Bhadrakālī, Komalini, Malikā, and Lakāli.
Kālāṅgī, Kāladūtī, Piśācī, Mārucisūcī, Piśācendrikā,
Koṭarākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Viṣadraṣṭī,
Viṣodbhavī, Subhagī, Darbhagī, Sukeśī, Vikeśī, Akraśyā, Aśvanāsī, Kuśāṇḍī.
She who wields the sword, the destroyer of Vetālas,
naked, five-faced, with a slender waist, wearing a garland of skulls, intoxicated by the liquor of Śrāvaṇī, her neck fierce with pride, and her head shaven— [she is] the one whose sword is [raised].
[There were] Tivirūpākṣi, Grāvīvikā, Viṭaṭālujāṅghī, Vikaṣuṇī, Vasodarī, Pūrṇakeśī, and Kuṇḍaladarśanī;

[and] the Piśācas named Śvabhakṣī and Piśitāśin, and hosts of Piśācas; and the eight great Nāgas named Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Ārkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Gulika; and those dwelling in cities, among the Nāgas, as Nāga-women, as Nāga-youths, on mountains, in Gandharva-difficult-to-reach places, and in forests.

(2nd line) And the winds of the womb-fire, the touch-wind, the blue world-wind, the life-force wind, the lord-of-life wind, the individual-soul wind, the pacifying wind, and the hosts of immortality-winds;
(3rd line)

And there were hosts of celestial damsels whose forms were as fierce as the downpour from clouds with eyes wide open due to the force of their sighs; and various showers of nectar, slow-moving, drawing away darkness, bearing names such as *Padavinyāsa* and *Padanāma*; and [beings] dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.
(5th line) And all the hosts of winds— accompanied by these, together with the entire multitude of winds from the northern and western quarters of the universe,
surrounded by four hundred thousand and ten million [attendants], come swiftly to this sacrifice with thousands. (f40.b 1st line)
O Vāyu, partake of this oblation; may you protect us always with blessings. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyu, the abode; salutation to the form of Vāyu.

(First line) He who is full, green-hued, possessing a banner of wind, the light, the bearer of the deer-banner, the life-force of all beings, the self of all beings, and the one with the golden deer-marked banner—Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyu.

(2nd line) Salutations to Jyavāyu; Svāhā! I offer this oblation. [I worship him] whose essence is as sweet as a rutting elephant, whose body is as lofty as a lotus, and who is adorned with earrings that shimmer like bees due to the swarms of bees drawn by the fragrance of the mass of blossoms stirred by the wind from his outstretched palms. (3rd–4th lines) He is one whose ears are graced by these earrings resembling lovely bees, which are formed from the collection of flowers shaken by the breeze from his expanded palms. (4th line) He is the one adorned with earrings that possess the beauty of bees, produced from the heap of flowers tossed by the wind from his opened palms. (4th line) He is the one wearing earrings decorated by the lovely bees attracted to the multitude of flowers by the breeze from his blossoming palms.
