With hands playing the *ḍamaru* drum, moving slowly upon the surface of the earth in the joy of dance, with limbs most charming and beautiful with tinkling bells,
with feet like lotuses tawny as gold, and with a throat perfectly suited to the sweet resonance of a multitude of gems, he is intent on a dance that is both graceful and majestic.

The *jampuṭa* [composition] is characterized by the doubling of syllables (*śrutipada*) at every step upon the surface of the earth, resulting in a quality multiplied by the number of folds in a bodice (*kañcuka*); it possesses the grace of the serpent-dance on Mount Rāmagiri, where the mountain peaks are bent like palm trees, and it is accompanied by the sound of the leaf-clapping of Śiva.

"Thus do I make the proclamation with the sound of the drum from the army of Śaṅkarasena"—this is the Vāyusandhi (the fourth line). Homage to the Lord of Wealth, the ruler of Namolakā; homage again and again to Kubera, the accountant of the Supreme Lord.

I pay homage to Candraśikha, the beloved friend of Maṇi, the son of Pulastya, who— through the effortless and constant practice of the limbs of compassion— is skilled in the mastery of the mind and the senses; he who dwells upon the slopes of Mount Dīrgha, possessing a wondrous and manifold splendor.
Mounted upon his horse-vehicle, bearing a sword, adorned with jewels and other ornaments, holding a bow white as cow’s milk, and dressed in red garments—
[he was] being served by hosts of Gandharvas, gods, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas at the command of the Lord of Gods, on the peak of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva).
Furthermore, Kubera, whose power is renowned through his friendship with the four-faced Brahmā, Hari, Viriñca, and other gods, who is difficult for even Śakra and others to behold,
and who is worshipped by the entire host of deities presiding over the treasures such as Śaṅkha and Padma— (3rd line)— [is also present].

Seated upon a footstool of honor, he was devoted to strolling in the regions of the Citraratha garden— renowned for its diverse and variegated splendors— while his matchless fame for beauty was sung by hosts of Puṇyajanas.
He whose staff-like arms are adorned, who dwells in the city of Alakāvatī, whose hand is eager to bestow the prosperity of the entire world upon the goddess Nṛndhi,
who is the beloved of Śraddhā, whose roar is deep as a thundercloud, who is mounted upon his vehicle Nandana, and who is joined by the rhythmic clapping of hands by the most skillful Gandharvas.
Delighting in the Mālavī and Tarkara rāgas and musical notes, he is one who upholds the command of the Supreme Lord; he is the northern Aśoka-Kubera, the great delighter of Nārada and Prahlāda.
[He who is] the one whose tongue is the fire of the sun, who was gazed upon by Kāla, [he who is like] Śaṅkhakarṇa, Śaṅkhodara, Śiśupāla, Dundubhi, Tāśaka, and the incarnation of Jvālāmālin;

[he who is] like a drop of water in the ocean, dear to the lineage of Sika, the essence of Mandāra and Saṃhikeya, the all-auspicious one, dear to happiness, the destroyer of pride, and the bestower of silence.

(4th line) O you who cause the destruction of Mantra, Hārimadana, Sainya, Karavikaṭa, and Hāsa; O you whose form is the source [of emanation]; O Kuṇḍeśī; O you who possess the nature of the thirty gods; O you who crush Akṣa and Puṣkara!
(5th line)
And the hosts of deities known as Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Narendravaśendra, Kuhāṇḍa, Vihāṇḍa, Virūpākṣa, Vaiśravaṇa,
Vāścikeya, Hayashrī, Vajambila, Śubhagarbha, Indriya, Dhautamāla, Vibudhapravṛtta, Dhūta, Sāṣṭra, Satada, and Asuracitta.
And the hosts of Siddhas named Karṣaṇa, Meṣacittakara, Kīsaṅgītamukhya, Sahyatalabhoga, Madanakaraṇa, and Abhidhāna,
as well as Pālikāvāyu— (line 2)

And the hosts of attendants—Śrīvajra, Māliketu, Mālīdhṛtarāṣṭra, and others; Sārasvata, Talasumukha, Supriya, Praveśana, Vainateya, Mekhanāda, Aśvattha, Puṣṭa, Supuṣṭa, Mahābala, and so forth; as well as those who sing of the yoga that knows the reality of the path of yoga.
And the yogins named Bhūṣita, Duṣṭamardana, Śiṣṭaparipālana, Śiva, Rudra, Mahāviṣṇu, Vāyu, Dharma, Candra, Sūrya, and others;
and the hosts of Kinnaras named Vīṇāvādya, Kinnara, Kiṃpuruṣa, Gīta, Śūrasena, Apramardana, and Gītā; and Sulocana—[all these were present].

And there were hosts of *vidyādhara* demons, possessing great fame, who had attained various branches of knowledge through the grace of those wise masters of the Vedas who were intent on the playful arts; they were of gentle nature, their very forms being like the fragrance of lotuses placed upon lovely *saugandhika* flower-vines, and they were perpetually festive.

And all the hosts of Kubera— the Daityas, Asuras, Dānavas, Piśācas, Bhakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and others— along with those dwelling in the celestial realms, the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworlds (Tālātala),
surrounded by their entire retinues, have assembled here before you, having offered their minds and bodies.
May we, being supported, obtain offspring. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kubera; obeisance to the form of Kubera.
[I worship] Kubera, seated upon a man, possessing a proud yet dwarfed body, with hands holding a golden club, the lord of the northern quarter.
One should remember: *Oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ*.

With the mantra *kuberāya svāhā*, I offer this oblation (*bali*). May there be immediate prosperity, the brilliance of the white water-lily, a shimmering and auspicious abundance, and the fulfillment of all wealth.

Eternally seated upon the lotus of his navel, with eyes directed toward the unfolding of the entire creation, he is the one who has entered into the assembly of perfected beings, renowned sages, and ascetics; he is the eternal, well-determined, and auspiciously resting Lord.

He is the one who protects, whose nature is eternally manifest as the elements of existence, and who is filled with a multitude of diverse, praiseworthy, and beautiful deeds—abounding in reality, wondrous, and sublime.

O Śaṅkarasena, commander-in-chief, I [perform] the *pañcatāla* drum-beating for the lord’s kettle-drum— a performance praised as beautiful, with rhythmic movements of the hands and feet, accompanied by the *mākujcita* and *parṇatarkarāga* melodies.
I perform the proclamation. Thus ends the section on Kubera.
(5th line) Homage to you who hold the trident in your hand; homage to the one with the blue throat. Homage to the God of gods, to the Lord; repeated homage to Śrīvābhūṣa. (6th line)

Together with his attendants, I repeatedly salute Īśāna, the moon-crested Lord, who possesses a multitude of terrifying serpents, whose weapons are the *huṃkāra* and the *ṭaṅka*, whose lofty banner flutters, whose form is radiant, whose head is smeared with ashes, who is praised by the objects of the senses, and who has three eyes.

The Lord of the Mountain (Īśāna), whose nature is that of Īśāna, who resembles a pure crystal, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods, who is endowed with the eight forms beginning with Vyoma, and who is adorned with a mass of matted locks coiled upon his right shoulder— having arrived at the mountain for the festival, he is to be worshipped by the hosts of Gaṇas by the command of the Lord of Gods; his pair of lotus-feet are saluted by all the gods and asuras, and [he is bathed] by the rays of the crescent moon.
His forehead-marked brow bore the shimmering play of fresh, reddish droplets from the fragrant water flowing from the tips of the crowns of the *sumita* flowers in his matted locks;
his neck was adorned with the lovely blackness of the wind-blown dust from the mountains of the Maruts and Paṇis.

His natural form and attire consist of the characteristics of similarity with Nīlakaṇṭha obtained through his grace; he is white in color like a cloud of autumn, dwells in the city of Yaśovatī, and has the bull as his emblem.
He whose weapon is the trident that severs the pride of the enemies of the gods; who delights in the sounds of the *ḍakkā*, *karaṭāla*, and *kumbha* drums;
whose eyes are like the *bhramarika* region and the *parṇaśālā*; who is dear to the voice;
and who is protected by the command of the Supreme Lord—[he is] the North-Eastern Quarter.

Īśāna [is the lord] of Meru, Mandara, Niṣadha, Kailāsa, Ratnakūṭa, Citrakūṭa, Mūdakūṭa, Lokāloka, Śrīśaila, Malaya, Mālyācala, Aruṇācala, Gandhamādana, and other divine mountains; as well as the Brahmāstra, Viṣṇuvāstra, and Śivāstra.
The Aghora-weapon, the Pāśupata-weapon, the Kṣurikā-weapon, the Patyaṅgirā-weapon, the Vīra-weapon, and the hosts of divine weapons;
and the eight forms known as Earth, Fire, Sacrifice... [f45a, line 1] ...Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Sky; and Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, and Īśāna.

Bhīma, Mahādeva, and Abhidāna; the lords of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti); the hundred Rudras beginning with Kapālīśa; the eleven Rudras beginning with Mahādeva; Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta; and the five Brahmans consisting of the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, Eye, Weapon, Conquest, and Bestowal.
The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, the eight lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) beginning with Ananta,
the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) beginning with Pradhāna and Pṛthivī,
and [the seats] such as Anantāsana, Yogāsana, Padmāsana, Vīrāsana, Vilōsana, Kūrmāsana, Kukkuṭāsana, and so forth.

The hosts of Sanakas and all the classes of gods beginning with the Viśvāmaras; Maheśvara, Kārttikeya, Nandi, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Skanda, Devī, Caṇḍeśvara, the one named Abhidāna, Kṣetrapāla, Piṇḍadi, Dīrghasauvarṇa, Sthāṇu, Rudra, Caturvaktra, Nikumbha, and Kumbhoda.
O you whose hair is like lightning, whose eyes are a mass of flames, who are golden-hued, the comet of smoke, the thousand-headed one, Kumbhakarṇa, Viṣambha, the moon-faced one,
the limit of the Lokāloka mountain, the golden-eared one, and Death!
O Great Illusion consisting of a hundred faces that remove the poison of Kālakiṅkiṇī and Kākapāda;
O you who are the mountain-ornament and the eight ornaments of all malevolent Piśācas;
O you whose mind’s expansion causes Meru to fall, [you who destroy] all sins...
...and the leaders of the Pramatha hosts, such as Naṣṭa, Śiṣṭa, Spasta, Suramardaka, and others; the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā);
the states of Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and Sāyujya; and all those residing in the celestial realms, the atmosphere, the earth, Pātāla, and Atala.
...and the hosts of *nāgas*— together with these [beings]— [worship] the Blessed One, the cause of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of the entire world.

O Pārvatī, on the thirteenth day of the festival of the raising of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*) for the sake of serving the auspicious Kalyāṇa-tīrtha of the illustrious Ekāmranātha— who, together with Ambā Kāmākṣī, is the playful diversion of the Lord— I, protected by the command of the Supreme Lord, [established] the northeast quarter of Īśāna’s...ṇa.

(4th line) Surrounded by his assembly, we praise that Īśāna, the Lord of the universe, who quickens our intellects for our protection. We pray to Pūṣan, who, through his wisdom, may be present among us; he is the guardian and protector, wielding the staff for our well-being. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Īśāna; Oṃ hāṃ, Īśāna.

(6th line) Salutation to the Embodiment; [I worship] Īśāna, mounted upon a bull, bearing a trident and a serpent, having a form like the new moon, with the moon as his crest-jewel, and three eyes. (f46.b, 1st line)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna; with "jya īśāya svāhā," I offer this oblation.
[I salute] the one whose conch-like ears are praised by the lotus-born Brahmā, who wears a beautiful chariot adorned with tinkling bells and a hundred bracelets, and whose vehicle is a lotus.

May that auspicious one, who wears earrings, whose face is like the orb of the moon, who has a hundred heads, who drinks the ocean, who is the abode of the multitude of Shiva’s prostrations, who is praised by the virtuous, and who destroys the cycle of rebirth— may he grant us well-being.

(4th line) The *tāla* in the *ḍakarī* rāga, the *deśākṣi* dance with feet raised, the leaf-hut hand gesture, and the *kumbha* drum— thus, by the command of Caṇḍeśvara, the commander of Śaṅkara’s army, [the sounds of] the mṛdaṅga, vīṇā, flute, *phaṇava*, *tālaka*, and *kāhala* [resounded]. (6th line)
"I shall cause the drum to resound here with the loud proclamations of the Saṅghapāha," thus says the junction of Īśāna.
